projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Alma Fisher was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Victoria Brandis
sp.p: What inspired you to be an army nurse?

sp.speaker: Alma Fisher
sp.p: Well, this was after Pearl Harbor, and I was working in the Philadelphia Lion Inn. And one of my friends said, "Let's join the army. They need nurses." So we went to the Red Cross, signed up, and then got orders to report to Camp Pickett, Virginia. And I started there on the third of January, 1943.

sp.speaker: Victoria Brandis
sp.p: How much training had you received before you enlisted?

sp.speaker: Alma Fisher
sp.p: I was an RN (registered nurse)....a professional RN.

sp.speaker: Victoria Brandis
sp.p: Did you receive further training once you enlisted.

sp.speaker: Alma Fisher
sp.p: I wasn't enlisted, I was an officer, so there's a difference there too.

sp.speaker: Victoria Brandis
sp.p: Would you be able to explain this difference?

sp.speaker: Alma Fisher
sp.p: The enlisted men... .well, it is like the president and the secretary. The president would be the officer, and the secretary would be the ordinary person. The officer gives the orders to the person below them.

sp.speaker: Victoria Brandis
sp.p: What different areas were you stationed at while you were serving?

sp.speaker: Alma Fisher
sp.p: Well, I started at Camp Pickett, Virginia. I can't remember how long I was there. This is during the war, we were sent to a staging area in Oran, Africa. We were where they called it Rock Hill, which was really a staging area, where you're waiting for fiirther orders to transfer to somewhere else. We lived in tents... .we wore men's' clothes and [ ? ]. Our underwear we washed in the helmets; the same one we took a bath iiL Eventually they set up showers, with a canvas around and showers overhead. I don't know how long we stayed there, but then we were assigned to the 78* Station Hospital, and we went to Bizante (Tunisia), which is in Africa. We were one of four hospitals situated along "Hospital Row." We took care of German and Italian soldiers, which were prisoners. And lived and worked in tents. You learned to make do with make-shift equipment; and a nurse is always a nvirse. After a certain period of time, we moved to Naples, Italy. And here we took over an Italian Army Garrison and made it into a hospital. And now here again we took care of Italian and German prisoners of war. And then after that, we again moved to a half-hour outside of Cannes, France. It was a TB Sanitarium. It overlooked the Mediterranean Sea and the Alps in the background. We took care of United States soldiers.. ..and there were soldiers from the Italian front, the Battle of the Bulge, and I can't remember the other outfits....the wounded soldiers that came back from the frontlines. And then after the war, when the war was declared ended, we were sent to Marselle, France. Waited at the staging area there. Waited to return to the United States. And then I was discharged on December 17, 1945. Along came the Korean War, and I was called back to active duty on February 12, 1951. I served at the following units: the United States Army Hospital in Camp Pickett, VA, United States Army Hospital in Okinawa, the United States Army Hospital in fort Carson, Colorado (Colorado Springs), the United States Army Hospital in Hanford, Washington, the United States Army Hospital in La Rochelle, France, the US Army Hospital in Fort Sam Houston, Texas, and then I went to the 14* Field Hospital in Bad Breuznach, Germany.. .the United States Army Hospital in Fort Belvoir, Virgmia. I retired June 30th 1970...serving 22 years, four months, and two days.

sp.speaker: Victoria Brandis
sp.p: When you were serving during World War Two, you said you were taking care of Italian and German prisoners of war, can you describe what that was like dealing with prisoners of war?

sp.speaker: Alma Fisher
sp.p: They were just Uke American boys. They were very happy and gratefiil to be there. They never had it so good.

sp.speaker: Victoria Brandis
sp.p: Was there ever any threats?

sp.speaker: Alma Fisher
sp.p: Nope, they were happy.

sp.speaker: Victoria Brandis
sp.p: You described living in tents, could you please describe what the hospitals were like?

sp.speaker: Alma Fisher
sp.p: They were just big tents, with all these cots down there. And soldiers there on the beds, and then you'd use fiioiit crates as bedside tables, and it was just like a makeshift hospital, is what it is.

sp.speaker: Victoria Brandis
sp.p: The living conditions in the hospitals, you described about doing your laundry in the helmets...

sp.speaker: Alma Fisher
sp.p: Yeah, this was in Africa. I don't remember what we did, how we did it in France and Italy; I don't remember. But at that pomt,.. .this was in the staging area when we lived, nurses all lived in one big tent. It must have been about 2-3 dozen in one tent. And we used to take showers...when they fixed up the showers...and there's no place to do the personal laundry. So after we took our.. .before we had the showers, we always did our personal laundry in our hehnets, because we had no place else to do it. As I said, you learned to make the best of things, and do the best you can.. .oh it was quite an experience!

sp.speaker: Victoria Brandis
sp.p: How did most nurses react to these initial changes in living conditions?

sp.speaker: Alma Fisher
sp.p: Well, we all accepted it. What else could you do? Because that was expected of us. We knew we weren't gonna hve in a palace. And when we were young, we could do it.

sp.speaker: Victoria Brandis
sp.p: What sort of medical equipment did you have to work with?

sp.speaker: Alma Fisher
sp.p: Not much of anything.. .the hospital had an X-ray, they had an operating room, and then they'd have the wards...these big tents, with patients in it. It was just like a hospital ward.

sp.speaker: Victoria Brandis
sp.p: What sort of responsibilities did nurses have through out the day?

sp.speaker: Alma Fisher
sp.p: It was just like an ordinary hospital here in the US. It was the same thing. You'd give out pills.. .1 can't remember. The men that needed wound dressings, we would dress...

sp.speaker: Victoria Brandis
sp.p: What sort of medications or anesthesia was available for the soldiers?

sp.speaker: Alma Fisher
sp.p: I don't remember, probably ether. 'Cause I wasn't in the operating room.

sp.speaker: Victoria Brandis
sp.p: What were your particular things that you did, then?

sp.speaker: Alma Fisher
sp.p: It was like you'd be in the medical ward back here in the United States. It's no different. You take care of medical patients like you would here in the States. It's no different...it was just the conditions you worked under. Instead of a regular building, you had a tent...

sp.speaker: Victoria Brandis
sp.p: What sort of devices or medical routines occurred?

sp.speaker: Alma Fisher
sp.p: I can't remember. I just don't know.

sp.speaker: Victoria Brandis
sp.p: Well, could you describe the living conditions for each day?

sp.speaker: Alma Fisher
sp.p: Well, you lived in tents. You slept on cots. On top of that cot, you had the bed roll, which you stored all your clothes in. And you put your blankets and sheets on top of that, and slept on that. And then there's four people to a tent, and in the middle of that, there's a pot [belly?] stove. I think it was heated with oil, but I'm not sure. But once we got into France, they had a TB (Tuberculosis) Hospital there, which was a building. And you had the same thing...you had big wards with wounded soldiers, which you took care of This was so long ago, that I just don't remember.

sp.speaker: Victoria Brandis
sp.p: How often did you get to work in a hospital versus a plane or ship?

sp.speaker: Alma Fisher
sp.p: I didn't. The only time I was on a ship, was coming back to the states.

sp.speaker: Victoria Brandis
sp.p: How did local disease affect the troops or the nurse?

sp.speaker: Alma Fisher
sp.p: Pardon?

sp.speaker: Victoria Brandis
sp.p: Were there many local disease or...

sp.speaker: Alma Fisher
sp.p: No; in Africa we had tents and nets over the beds, so we wouldn't get malaria. But outside of that.. .1 mean.. .1 don't know what we did when we got sick. I don't know.

sp.speaker: Victoria Brandis
sp.p: What sort of precautions were taken on a daily basis for possible drills and such?

sp.speaker: Alma Fisher
sp.p: None.

sp.speaker: Victoria Brandis
sp.p: Could you describe then the relations amongst doctors and nurses? Or between the nurses and soldiers?

sp.speaker: Alma Fisher
sp.p: Well, doctors acted the same way towards the patients as your doctor treats you. There's no difference. The nurses and the doctors were the same way as here in the US...

sp.speaker: Victoria Brandis
sp.p: How close were you to the battlefields?

sp.speaker: Alma Fisher
sp.p: We were miles behind it. Miles behind it. When we were in Bizante, we were in a tent hospital there. I don't remember how many miles behind at Bizante. But we were anyways well behind the lines.

sp.speaker: Victoria Brandis
sp.p: Bizante?

sp.speaker: Alma Fisher
sp.p: Bizante is the name of the town (in Africa), which is up and along the Mediterranean Coast. It's in Africa. It's up there. And then there's a port there, which Jerry (the Germans) used to come up there at night, and drop flares and bombs there at the port, which we could see from where we worked and lived. But they dropped one dud bomb at our area, but fortunately, it was a dud, and it didn't explode. So otherwise I wouldn't be here today...

sp.speaker: Victoria Brandis
sp.p: How would you go about getting supplies and food?

sp.speaker: Alma Fisher
sp.p: Well, that was the quartermaster's job. They had a department in the army for the quartermaster, which supplied all the food. Bought all the food, took care of the laimdry, and was responsible for bringing in all the supplies.

sp.speaker: Victoria Brandis
sp.p: How did shortages affect you?

sp.speaker: Alma Fisher
sp.p: For the States, we didn't. We always got priority.

sp.speaker: Victoria Brandis
sp.p: What about when you were in Africa or in Europe, were there often shortages?

sp.speaker: Alma Fisher
sp.p: Nope. The Army got priority in everything. What the army wanted, the army got. So they talked about sugar shortages, butter shortages in the United States, we never were...

sp.speaker: Victoria Brandis
sp.p: Would you be able to describe the different stations that were set out along the fields, or behind the fields for the hospitals?

sp.speaker: Alma Fisher
sp.p: Out in the war zone, you had your First Aid Station. Behind that...I forget. Then there were the field hospitals. There was something in between there, I don't remember what. And then behind that, you had the station hospitals. And then somewhere near the front lines, the worst cases were flown back to the general hospitals, if there were any in that particular area...and there were very few. And the ones they couldn't handle, were shipped back to the United States.

sp.speaker: Victoria Brandis
sp.p: What sort of different stations would you find in these hospitals?

sp.speaker: Alma Fisher
sp.p: It depends. These hospitals, some were surgical hospitals. We were prison hospitals. There were some psychiatric hospitals; so each had their own specialty.

sp.speaker: Victoria Brandis
sp.p: How different were the environments, from that between the prisoner hospitals or the psychiatric hospitals?

sp.speaker: Alma Fisher
sp.p: None as far as I know. I mean, we're all out there in the middle of the field out there, set up in these tents, and there you were. Because up in Bizante, we were in the middle of a wheat field. And we set up the tents in this wheat field. The large tents were the hospitals, and the smaller tents were where the personnel lived.

sp.speaker: Victoria Brandis
sp.p: How often were you able to stay in these makeshift hospitals with tents?

sp.speaker: Alma Fisher
sp.p: Well the whole thing is, I stayed two years overseas. Two years back in the states. Two years overseas overseas, two years back in the states. And that's the way it rotated til my final end [?].

sp.speaker: Victoria Brandis
sp.p: How much did each hospital move around? Aima: That depends upon the war condition. That depended solely on the war conditions.

sp.speaker: Victoria Brandis
sp.p: So at anytime...

sp.speaker: Alma Fisher
sp.p: We could jxist pick up and leave. We got orders to pick up and leave. It depended solely on how the war was goin...were they safe to move this outfit forward, or stay there or what? This is how it worked. They cleared an area...say we're in Africa, ok...they cleared an area which they felt was far back behind the lines enough that they could stage a hospital or something. Because they always kept the hospitals way behind the lines, so we weren't anywhere near dmiger.

sp.speaker: Victoria Brandis
sp.p: Who was responsible for moving all these hospitals?

sp.speaker: Alma Fisher
sp.p: That came from Washington, DC.

sp.speaker: Victoria Brandis
sp.p: Who set up the actual hospitals and stuff? Was it the nurses...

sp.speaker: Alma Fisher
sp.p: No, we had nothing to do with it. Those orders came from higher headquarters, because you got your orders from higher headquarters, and then they'd direct you what to do. Because the hospital commander does not make decisions on his own. He's given orders to do this and orders to do that.

sp.speaker: Victoria Brandis
sp.p: Personally, would nurses just switch from hospital to hospital or would the hospitals...

sp.speaker: Alma Fisher
sp.p: No, you are stationed to a hospital, and you move with that hospital. Like in World war two, I was with this.. ..78* Station Hospital, so I went with the 78* to Africa, France, Italy, and then came back as a unit, and was discharged from Fort Dicks. So the hospital unit stays together through the whole, because it'd be too confixsing and too mixed up if you changed the personnel.

sp.speaker: Victoria Brandis
sp.p: You talked about the different supplies you used in these hospitals, how would they differ between, let's say, Africa and the European places?

sp.speaker: Alma Fisher
sp.p: That was the responsibility of transportation. You see, the army has a transportation area, a quartermaster area, they have a 'this' area. So each section has its own. The quartermasters supply the food and the clothes. The transportation worries about getting you from here to there.

sp.speaker: Victoria Brandis
sp.p: How were the living conditions different? Were they similar or...

sp.speaker: Alma Fisher
sp.p: Well it depends where you were stationed. I mean, down in the fields, you're living in tents. And then when we got to France and Italy, we were in a building. But see, you take over the building, which belonged to the country you're in, and then you make the best of whatever you're assigned to.

sp.speaker: Victoria Brandis
sp.p: Can you describe some of the difficulties that the nurses in the hospitals had, in putting together these makeshift hospitals?

sp.speaker: Alma Fisher
sp.p: It was out of our hands.

sp.speaker: Victoria Brandis
sp.p: But what sort of difficulties would you encounter?

sp.speaker: Alma Fisher
sp.p: I don't know; I don't think we had any.

sp.speaker: Victoria Brandis
sp.p: How large or small were these hospitals, the makeshift hospitals?

sp.speaker: Alma Fisher
sp.p: I couldn't tell ya; because I don't know how many patients we had. I don't know how many patients other so-called hospitals had. I just don't know.

sp.speaker: Victoria Brandis
sp.p: Were there just a few tents or many tents?

sp.speaker: Alma Fisher
sp.p: I don't know. I can't remember.

sp.speaker: Victoria Brandis
sp.p: How frequent did the soldiers seem to turn over?

sp.speaker: Alma Fisher
sp.p: I don't know that either, because the one's I had weren't that badly wounded. I think the most were medical patients.

sp.speaker: Victoria Brandis
sp.p: Could you please describe what you meant be "just medical patients?"

sp.speaker: Alma Fisher
sp.p: Well, they had colds, malaria, medical situations...not surgical. I mean, they weren't surgical, they were medical...pneumonia, colds, stuff like that. Flu.

sp.speaker: Victoria Brandis
sp.p: What sort of medications would you use to give them?

sp.speaker: Alma Fisher
sp.p: Well, that was before the days of penicillin, before sulpha. Sulpha.. .this was back m World War Two, and we just didn't have all this modern stuff like they have today. It was unheard of It wasn't invented.

sp.speaker: Victoria Brandis
sp.p: How would you go about taking care of them then, without the modern medications?

sp.speaker: Alma Fisher
sp.p: (laughing) I don't remember. Fortunately, they were young guys and they weren't that sick. We had malaria pills, that I know. But they weren't that ill, really.

sp.speaker: Victoria Brandis
sp.p: Dealing with strictly prisoners of war, were you able to communicate a lot with them?

sp.speaker: Alma Fisher
sp.p: Oh yea. We used...some understood some English. And then we'd use the sign language (making gestures with her hands). And the little bit of German I knew, I tried that out. I knew a few words in Italian. I mean, usually someone else might help you out.

sp.speaker: Victoria Brandis
sp.p: Were there any sorts of problems that arose?

sp.speaker: Alma Fisher
sp.p: No, no, no. I said they were happy and content. They were glad to be out of the war. And they were well taken care of

sp.speaker: Victoria Brandis
sp.p: How was the interaction? Was it a lot of friendly interaction or institutional interaction?

sp.speaker: Alma Fisher
sp.p: ... We wouldn't become friendly with them. You'd act very professional. I mean, that's it. There's a line you draw.

sp.speaker: Victoria Brandis
sp.p: Were there ever coincidences where it was stepped over that line?

sp.speaker: Alma Fisher
sp.p: No, you'd be careful it didn't happen.

sp.speaker: Victoria Brandis
sp.p: How so? Can you describe what might have happened if you did change your interaction?

sp.speaker: Alma Fisher
sp.p: (Pause) Well, I don't know. You'd treat 'em as if you're the doctor, and they're the patient. It's the same way your doctor treats you, or your nurse in the doctor's office treats you. There's still that line, that you don't become friendly with 'em at all. I mean, you're polite to them, and you're kind to them, but you don't try to make friends with them.

sp.speaker: Victoria Brandis
sp.p: Well thank you very much for this interview.

sp.speaker: Alma Fisher
sp.p: You're quite welcome. I'm sorry, it's been so long, and I just don't remember.

sp.speaker: Victoria Brandis
sp.p: No problem at all. And I'm just going to give you this release form, which says that basically you agree that this information can be shared.
